summary:
What we developed: a 12-slide pitch deck for a concept called PolarView, a web tool for comparing lunar south pole landing sites and dates. We built the presentation and an interface mock-up, not a working application. The chart numbers and Sites A/B/C are illustrative.
How it addresses the challenge:
Simple interface: pick sites, drag a date timeline, and read the result on one screen, replacing complicated tool interfaces.
Sun and Earth vs. the horizon: a sky view draws both over the local terrain horizon.
Power: a timeline shows sunlit windows and long dark gaps.
Communications: a second timeline shows when Earth is above the horizon for direct-to-Earth links.
Quick comparison: side-by-side site bars let planners, educators and the public compare options in seconds.
Feasible build: it uses public NASA data (SPICE ephemerides, LRO LOLA terrain), with the heavy computation done in advance so the browser stays fast.
Why it matters:
At Artemis candidate regions the Sun never rises above about 7°, so shadows are long and sunlight comes and goes.
Without relays, a lander needs Earth in view, so power and communications decide which sites and dates are workable.
A fast, visual tool helps planners shortlist options sooner, and it lets students and the public understand the pole's unusual lighting
details:
What it does and how it works

PolarView is a web tool that lets mission planners, educators and the public compare lunar south pole landing sites and dates in seconds. The user picks one or more sites and drags a date timeline. The tool then draws the Sun and Earth over the site's real terrain horizon. Two timelines show sunlit periods for power and Earth-visible periods for direct-to-Earth communication. Sun and Earth positions come from NASA ephemerides. Each site's horizon comes from lunar terrain data. The tool compares each body's elevation to the horizon at its direction. The heavy calculations are done in advance, so the browser responds instantly.

Benefits

It replaces complicated interfaces with one clear screen.

Side-by-side comparison speeds up site and date shortlisting.

Power and communication trade-offs are visible at a glance.

It runs in any browser with no install, so non-experts can use it too.

Intended impact

Help teams choose landing sites and dates faster and with more confidence. It also makes the pole's extreme lighting (the Sun never above about 7° at candidate regions) understandable to students and the public.

Tools and technology (planned stack)

Data: NASA NAIF SPICE kernels for Sun and Earth positions, and LRO LOLA topography for horizon profiles

Precomputation: Python with SpiceyPy

Front end: JavaScript with React and D3/Canvas, using static JSON files per site and static hosting

Pitch deck: pptxgenjs, a JavaScript library for building PowerPoint files

Creativity

The sky is shown as a horizon view, as a person on the surface would see it, instead of as tables of angles.

Power and comms windows sit on one shared timeline, so conflicts show up immediately.

One interface scales from expert planning to public education.

Factors considered

Accuracy: terrain horizons matter a lot at such low Sun angles.

Speed: precomputing keeps the interface fast.

Audience: three groups with different needs.

Data openness: only public NASA data is used.

Limits: no relay satellites are assumed, and coverage starts with a few sites before all 13 candidate regions.
